stages.name: Merger policy: advantages and disadvantages
stages.title: Merger policy: advantages and disadvantages
stages.sub: The student can weigh up whether merger control does more good than harm.

steps.q: Two of the four biggest supermarkets want to merge. The CMA blocks it because the combined firm would dominate the market. Who benefits from that decision?
steps.right: Consumers, because prices and choice are protected
steps.wrong: Consumers, because the merger would have cut costs for them
steps.hint: Think about what tends to happen to prices when one firm gets very dominant.
steps.pre: So blocking mergers that would create too much market power is an

steps.q: Two small van makers want to merge purely so they can buy parts in bulk and spread factory costs over more output, without becoming dominant. Should the CMA treat this the same as the supermarket merger that would crush rivals?
steps.right: No, this one can still be allowed to go ahead
steps.wrong: Yes, all mergers between competitors should be blocked
steps.hint: Does this merger reduce competition, or mainly just cut costs?
steps.pre: So being able to tell these two cases apart means merger policy is also an

steps.q: The CMA must decide today whether a merger will harm competition in five years, in a market that keeps changing, using only current evidence. Does it have full information about the future?
steps.right: No, only limited evidence to estimate from
steps.wrong: Yes, the future effects can be measured now
steps.hint: Is the CMA looking at data from the past, or trying to see into the future?
steps.pre: So the CMA faces real difficulty in

steps.q: Given that the CMA cannot know the future for certain, is there a risk it blocks a merger that would actually have been harmless, or approves one that turns out to harm competition?
steps.right: Yes, its decision could turn out to be wrong either way
steps.wrong: No, its economists can always get the decision right
steps.hint: If the evidence is limited, can the outcome still be predicted with certainty?

steps.q: Because of this difficulty in judging the future, the CMA runs a long, thorough investigation. A merger investigation takes 18 months and costs both firms millions in legal fees, even though it is eventually approved. What has that delay cost the firms and their customers?
steps.right: Time and money that a beneficial merger loses while waiting
steps.wrong: Nothing, since the merger was approved anyway
steps.hint: Even a merger that gets a yes still has to wait and pay for the investigation.
